results.name: tight_cluster_near_outside_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets 1-5 outside the example span (below min or above max) on sets of >=2 examples spanning <=10; observed > null means the model rejects targets just outside a tight cluster more than people do (overly strong size principle), observed < null means people are even tighter.
results.code:
# name: tight_cluster_near_outside_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets 1-5 outside the example span (below min or above max) on sets of >=2 examples spanning <=10; observed > null means the model rejects targets just outside a tight cluster more than people do (overly strong size principle), observed < null means people are even tighter.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    k = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    lo, hi = ex.min(axis=1), ex.max(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    d = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0))
    m = (k >= 2) & ((hi - lo) <= 10) & (d >= 1) & (d <= 5)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df.loc[m, "rating"].mean())

results.name: multiple_rule_beyond_span_contrast
results.description: In sets of >=3 examples all divisible by some m in 3..12 (not all powers of 2), among targets outside the example span, yes rate on multiples of m minus non-multiples; observed > null means people extend arithmetic rules beyond the examples' range more than the model, observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: multiple_rule_beyond_span_contrast
# description: In sets of >=3 examples all divisible by some m in 3..12 (not all powers of 2), among targets outside the example span, yes rate on multiples of m minus non-multiples; observed > null means people extend arithmetic rules beyond the examples' range more than the model, observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    k = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    lo, hi = ex.min(axis=1), ex.max(axis=1)
    outside = (t < lo) | (t > hi)
    p2 = (ex.isin({2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1)
    base = (k >= 3) & outside & ~p2
    yes_r, yes_o = [], []
    used = pd.Series(False, index=df.index)
    for m in [12, 11, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3]:
        allm = ((ex % m == 0) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1) & base & ~used
        used |= allm
        yes_r.append(df.loc[allm & (t % m == 0), "rating"])
        yes_o.append(df.loc[allm & (t % m != 0), "rating"])
    r, o = pd.concat(yes_r), pd.concat(yes_o)
    if len(r) == 0 or len(o) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r.mean() - o.mean())

results.name: prime_set_extension_contrast
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all primes, yes rate on non-example prime targets minus yes rate on non-prime odd targets; observed > null means people generalise along primality more than the model, observed < null means the model over-weights the primes rule.

results.name: same_last_digit_set_offrule_inspan_rate
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples that all end in the same digit, yes rate on targets inside the example span that do NOT end in that digit; observed > null means people fall back on the range more than the model (model over-commits to the ends-in-d rule), observed < null means they follow the rule more strictly.
results.code:
# name: same_last_digit_set_offrule_inspan_rate
# description: For sets of >=3 examples that all end in the same digit, yes rate on targets inside the example span that do NOT end in that digit; observed > null means people fall back on the range more than the model (model over-commits to the ends-in-d rule), observed < null means they follow the rule more strictly.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    k = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    ld = ex % 10
    same = (ld.max(axis=1) == ld.min(axis=1)) & (k >= 3)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    inspan = (t > ex.min(axis=1)) & (t < ex.max(axis=1))
    m = same & inspan & ((t % 10) != ld.min(axis=1))
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df.loc[m, "rating"].mean())

results.name: within_set_target_dispersion
results.description: Mean over sets (>=3 distinct targets) of the variance across targets of the per-(set,target) yes rate; observed > null means people's generalisation within a set is more sharply all-or-none across targets than the model's, observed < null means flatter.
results.code:
# name: within_set_target_dispersion
# description: Mean over sets (>=3 distinct targets) of the variance across targets of the per-(set,target) yes rate; observed > null means people's generalisation within a set is more sharply all-or-none across targets than the model's, observed < null means flatter.
def test_statistic(df):
    c = df.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].mean().reset_index()
    v = c.groupby("number_set")["rating"].agg(["var", "size"])
    v = v[v["size"] >= 3]
    return float(v["var"].mean())

results.name: powers_of_two_extension_contrast
results.description: In sets whose examples are all powers of 2, yes rate on non-example powers of 2 minus yes rate on other even targets; observed > null means people extend the powers-of-2 rule more selectively than the model, observed < null means the model over-commits to the rule.
results.code:
# name: powers_of_two_extension_contrast
# description: In sets whose examples are all powers of 2, yes rate on non-example powers of 2 minus yes rate on other even targets; observed > null means people extend the powers-of-2 rule more selectively than the model, observed < null means the model over-commits to the rule.
def test_statistic(df):
    p2 = {2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    allp2 = ex.isin(p2) | ex.isna()
    sel = allp2.all(axis=1) & (ex.notna().sum(axis=1) >= 2)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    inset = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    rule = sel & t.isin(p2) & ~inset
    other = sel & ~t.isin(p2) & (t % 2 == 0)
    if rule.sum() == 0 or other.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df.loc[rule, "rating"].mean() - df.loc[other, "rating"].mean())

results.name: unstructured_wide_set_nonmember_rate
results.description: Yes rate on non-example targets for sets of >=3 examples spanning >=60 that share no parity, no last digit and no divisor 3..12; observed > null means people accept more numbers than the model when the examples show no rule, observed < null means they reject more.
results.code:
# name: unstructured_wide_set_nonmember_rate
# description: Yes rate on non-example targets for sets of >=3 examples spanning >=60 that share no parity, no last digit and no divisor 3..12; observed > null means people accept more numbers than the model when the examples show no rule, observed < null means they reject more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    k = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    span = ex.max(axis=1) - ex.min(axis=1)
    shared = pd.Series(False, index=df.index)
    for m in range(2, 13):
        shared |= ((ex % m == 0) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1)
    shared |= ((ex % 2 == 1) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1)
    ld = ex % 10
    shared |= (ld.max(axis=1) == ld.min(axis=1))
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    inset = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    m = (k >= 3) & (span >= 60) & ~shared & ~inset
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df.loc[m, "rating"].mean())

results.name: order_effect_8_16
results.description: Yes rate for set "16,8" minus yes rate for set "8,16" over the targets both orders were asked about; the model is order-invariant (null ~0), so a nonzero observed value means presentation order changes generalisation (positive = descending order generalises more).
results.code:
# name: order_effect_8_16
# description: Yes rate for set "16,8" minus yes rate for set "8,16" over the targets both orders were asked about; the model is order-invariant (null ~0), so a nonzero observed value means presentation order changes generalisation (positive = descending order generalises more).
def test_statistic(df):
    a = df[df["number_set"] == "16,8"]
    b = df[df["number_set"] == "8,16"]
    common = set(a["target"]) & set(b["target"])
    if not common:
        return 0.0
    a = a[a["target"].isin(common)]
    b = b[b["target"].isin(common)]
    return float(a["rating"].mean() - b["rating"].mean())
